Traditional manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible do not have a marginal notation about this as they do in the case of 7:20, but many translations read “cursed” since this is the kind of change that scribes are known to have made in similar cases.

2:13: Job’s friends sat with him on the ground as a symbolic action to express their sincere sympathy with him.

Job assumes that his listeners will understand that by claim he is referring to the way, in his culture, a close relative would bring an orphaned child into his own home and make that child a member of his own family.
Job is speaking as if darkness and a dark shadow were living things that could adopt the day of his birth, as if it too were a living thing.

Job is speaking of a cloud as if it were a living thing that could dwell or make its home over the day of his birth, and he is speaking of that day as if it were something that itself lived in a particular place.

3:7: Job is speaking of the night he was conceived as if it were a living thing that could be barren. He means that he does not want that night to have any children, in the sense that he does not want any more children to be conceived on that night or, as the context suggests, born on that night.
Job is speaking of a joyful shout as if it were a living thing that could come into a place. He is referring to people shouting for joy on the night of the day when he was born.
Job means implicitly that he does not want anyone to shout joyfully on this particular night to celebrate the birth of a child.
3:8: Job assumes that his listeners will understand that by the ones cursing a day he is referring to sorcerers. People in this culture employed sorcerers in the belief that they could cause bad things to happen on a particular day to their enemies. For example, people might employ a sorcerer to try to ruin the day on which a person began an important journey or celebrated an important family occasion such as a wedding.

The implication is that if sorcerers created chaos by awakening the chaos monster, there would no longer be any distinction between days, and so the day of Job’s birth would no longer have a distinct identity.

As the introduction to Job explains, ancient peoples seem to have been aware of a large, fierce creature that lived in the ocean, which they called the “sea monster.” People in Job’s culture regarded the sea as the realm of watery chaos, and they associated this sea monster with that chaos. That is the association that Job is making here, calling the sea monster by the name Leviathan.
3:9: Job is speaking of the day of his birth as if it were a living thing that could wait for light to appear in the sky and see the dawn.
Job is referring to light flashing from eyes by association with the eyelids that open to reveal that flashing.

Eliphaz is speaking as if Job were literally drinking iniquity the way he would drink water. He means that Job eagerly and willingly does wrong things, the way thirsty people eagerly and willingly drink water.
15:19: לָהֶם לְבַדָּם נִתְּנָה הָאָרֶץ וְלֹא־עָבַר זָר בְּתוֹכָם

By them, Eliphaz means the “fathers” or ancestors whom he described in the previous verse, and by the land he probably means Edom and specifically his home city of Teman, which was renowned for its wisdom (see Jeremiah 49:7). By saying that only those ancestors lived there and no stranger passed among them, he means that their wisdom was not diluted by outside influences.
15:20: Eliphaz is using the term days to refer to a specific time.
Eliphaz means implicitly that a wicked person will be writhing in pain because God will be punishing him for his sin.
15:21: Eliphaz is using the term ears by association to mean hearing. By saying that the wicked person hears the sound of terrors, Eliphaz means by association that he experiences those terrors.
The word translated prosperity can also mean “peace.” Eliphaz could be describing: (1) how wicked people may become prosperous for a time; (2) how wicked people may enjoy peace for a time.
Eliphaz is describing how the wicked experience the destruction and loss of their property, and he is speaking of that destruction as if it were a living thing that comes upon the wicked.
15:22: Eliphaz is speaking as if this wicked person has literally gone to a place where there is darkness and as if that wicked person does not believe that he can return from there.
It is possible that this second part of the verse also describes what wicked people believe.
Eliphaz is using one kind of deadly weapon, the sword, by association to mean violent death.
15:23: Eliphaz is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general.
Eliphaz is using the term day to refer to a specific time.
Eliphaz is speaking as if this wicked person knows that a time is coming when there will literally be darkness during the day.
Eliphaz is using the expression at hand to mean “nearby,” and he means near in time rather than near in place.
15:24: Eliphaz is speaking of Distress and anguish as if they were living things that could terrify a wicked person.
The terms Distress and anguish mean similar things. Eliphaz is using the two terms together for emphasis.
15:25: When Eliphaz says that the wicked person has stretched out his hand, he means specifically that he has stretched out a hand that is holding a sword or some other weapon. In other words, this expression means to fight against someone.
15:26: יָרוּץ אֵלָיו בְּצַוָּאר בַּעֲבִי גַּבֵּי מָגִנָּיו
Eliphaz is speaking as if a wicked person would literally attack God in this way. He is actually making a comparison to describe the arrogant confidence with which a wicked person defies God.
This expression refers to the attitude of someone who is holding his neck straight and his head high, displaying arrogant confidence with his posture.

The word “boss” describes the outwardly rounded part of a shield. A warrior would face this part of the shield against an enemy, holding the shield by a handle inside the boss. If a shield had a thick boss, that would protect the warrior against blows from swords and spears, and it would also allow a warrior to use the shield to knock an opponent down and pin him to the ground.

Eliphaz speaks in this verse of the thickness of the shield that the wicked person would use against God, but in the next verse he indicates that the wicked person is actually “fat” and so not in shape physically for combat. So while Eliphaz seems to suggest here that the wicked person is a formidable foe, he actually means the opposite of what he is saying, as the next verse reveals.
15:27: כִּי־כִסָּה פָנָיו בְּחֶלְבּוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ פִּימָה עֲלֵי־כָסֶל
Eliphaz is using two parts of the wicked person, his face and his flanks, to indicate that his whole body is obese.
כִּי־כִסָּה פָנָיו בְּחֶלְבּוֹ וַיַּעַשׂ פִּימָה עֲלֵי־כָסֶל
The implication is that the wicked person has a face that is fat and flanks that have blubber because he overeats and lives indolently.
15:30: Eliphaz is speaking as if the wicked person were literally a plant or bush whose stalks a flame could dry up or burn up.
Eliphaz is speaking as if a hot wind that dried up plants were actually breath from God’s mouth.
Eliphaz is using the word depart to mean “die.” This is a mild way of referring to death.
15:32: Eliphaz assumes that Job will understand that by his day, he means the day for the wicked to die.

Eliphaz is continuing the image from the previous verse of the wicked person being like a plant or bush. He is speaking of this plant or bush being alive by association with the way that its branches would be green inside if it were alive.
15:33: יַחְמֹס כַּגֶּפֶן בִּסְרוֹ וְיַשְׁלֵךְ כַּזַּיִת נִצָּתוֹ

The point of these comparisons is that the wicked person will not be able to succeed in his endeavors. They will all end in failure, just as a grapevine may not be able to nourish its grapes and so they will fall off while they are still unripe, and just as an olive tree might lose its blossoms due to cold weather in the spring and not bear any fruit that year.
יַחְמֹס כַּגֶּפֶן בִּסְרוֹ וְיַשְׁלֵךְ כַּזַּיִת נִצָּתוֹ

Eliphaz speaks as if the grapevine itself would shake off its grapes and as if the olive tree itself would cast off its blossoms. He means that the grapes will drop from the vine and the blossoms will fall off the tree.
15:34: This could mean: (1) that godless people literally will have no children or that they will have no children who survive them; (2) that godless people will produce nothing of enduring value, as if they had no descendants.
Eliphaz is speaking as if fire would literally devour or eat up these tents. He means that fire would destroy them.
Eliphaz is using the term bribery by association to mean people who pay and demand bribes.
Eliphaz is speaking as if the tents of people who engage in bribery will literally burn up in a fire. He means that they will be destroyed by one means or another.
Eliphaz is using one possession of wicked people, the tents in which they live, to mean all of their possessions and their standing in the community.
15:35: הָרֹה עָמָל וְיָלֹד אָוֶן וּבִטְנָם תָּכִין מִרְמָה
Eliphaz is speaking as if wicked people were literally women who had trouble, iniquity, and deceit as their children. He means that wicked people produce these things in their lives.
16:3: הֲקֵץ לְדִבְרֵי־רוּחַ אוֹ מַה־יַּמְרִיצְךָ כִּי תַעֲנֶה
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is answering Eliphaz with his own words.
16:4: Job is using one part of himself and his friends, their souls, to mean all of them.
Job is using the term words to mean the things that he would say by using words.
To shake the head at someone is a symbolic action indicating disapproval.
16:5: For emphasis, Job is saying the opposite of what he means. He does not feel that his friends actually have been strengthening him or relieving him.
Job is using the terms mouth and lips by association to mean speaking.
16:6: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
16:8: וַתִּקְמְטֵנִי לְעֵד הָיָה וַיָּקָם בִּי כַחֲשִׁי בְּפָנַי יַעֲנֶה

Job is speaking as if his shriveled condition, his leanness, were a living thing that was serving as a witness and testifying against him. He means that people consider him to be guilty of sin because they believe that God is punishing him with a sickness that has made him lose weight.
Here the word face could mean: (1) Job himself, using one part of him to represent all of him; (2) Job’s reputation as a righteous person, in a specific sense of the word face.
16:9: Job is speaking as if God were literally a wild animal that had attacked and torn him.

Job is speaking as if God, whom he believes is acting towards him as an enemy, were literally sharpening his eyes, the way one would sharpen a sword in order to use it dangerously as a weapon. Job means that God is focusing his eyes intently on him to recognize ways to attack him further and to ensure that he, Job, does not escape.
16:10: Opening the mouth wide at someone was a symbolic action that expressed ridicule.
16:11: Here, hands represents the power and control that people have over something.
Job is speaking as if God were literally throwing him into the hands of the wicked. He means that God is abandoning him to whatever it is that wicked people would want to do to him.
16:12: Job is speaking as if God has literally shattered him, breaking him into many parts, and seized his neck and shaken him to pieces. He means that God has destroyed everything important in his life—his family, his health, and his possessions.
Job is speaking as if God has literally set him up as a target. (He continues this image in the first line of the next verse.) He means that it seems as if God has harmed him very intentionally.
16:13: Job is speaking as if archers whom God commands have literally surrounded him. He means that God has caused him to experience many different troubles.
יְפַלַּח כִּלְיוֹתַי וְלֹא יַחְמוֹל יִשְׁפֹּךְ לָאָרֶץ מְרֵרָתִי
Job means implicitly that these archers are seeking mercilessly to kill him by shooting their arrows into his vital organs.
יְפַלַּח כִּלְיוֹתַי וְלֹא יַחְמוֹל יִשְׁפֹּךְ לָאָרֶץ מְרֵרָתִי

Job does not mean that arrows have literally pierced his kidneys and liver. He is continuing the image of the archers to indicate that it feels to him as if God is mercilessly trying to kill him in a way that he could not possibly survive.
16:14: Job is speaking as if he were a defensive wall around a city and God was smashing openings or breaches in that wall. He means that the continual sufferings that he is experiencing are making him less and less able to be resilient.
This expression could mean: (1) that God is smashing openings in many different places in this wall (which represents Job).

Job is speaking as if God were literally running against him the way a warrior would run to attack an enemy soldier. Job is answering Eliphaz with his own words. In 15:26, Eliphaz used the same image to describe how wicked people oppose God.
16:15: Job is speaking as if he had literally sewn sackcloth onto his skin. He could mean: (1) that he is continually in mourning, as if he wore sackcloth (a sign of mourning) so frequently that it seemed to be sewn onto his skin; (2) that he actually has been wearing sackcloth (although the narrative at the beginning of the book does not say so) and it has stuck to his skin because of his boils, as if it were sewn to his skin.

People in the biblical culture used the horn of an animal to represent strength and honor. When they did, they would speak of humans as if they had horns like animals. For example, Psalm 112:9 says of the person who fears the Lord, “His horn rises high in honor.” Job is using the image in the opposite way to say that he is suffering disgrace.
16:16: Job is describing the fact that he has not been sleeping well, by association with the way that dark circles form around the eyes of someone who lacks sleep.
16:17: Job is using one part of himself, his hands, to mean all of him in the potential act of committing violence.

Job is speaking as if his prayer were literally pure, that is, as if it were a physical substance that had nothing else mixed in. He means that when he prays, he means just what he says and he has no other motives other than sincerely speaking with God.
16:18: Job is speaking to something that he knows cannot hear him, the Earth. He is doing that to show in a strong way how he feels about what has been happening to him.

Job is speaking as if he were literally going to be murdered and as if his blood were going to fall to the ground and soak into the earth unless something prevented that. He means that he is like the victim of a deadly crime in that he deserves justice but there is a risk that he will not receive it.

It is likely that Job is continuing to address the Earth in this part of the verse. Once again he is doing that in order to show in a strong way how he feels about what has been happening to him. The context makes clear that this is a cry for justice.
16:19: See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter to decide how to translate the terms witness and advocate, which both describe the same person, someone whom Job expects will intercede for him in heaven.
16:20: Job is using one part of himself, his eye, to mean all of him in the act of weeping.
16:22: When Job says that he will go on a path and not return, he means that he will die. This is a mild way of referring to death.
17:1: Job is making an overstatement when he says that his spirit has already been destroyed and his days have already been extinguished. He means that this is nearly the case.
This could mean: (1) Job’s life. Job would be using one part of himself, his spirit, to mean all of him; (2) Job’s strength and morale.
Job is using the term days to mean a specific period of time, his lifetime.
Job is speaking as if his life were literally a flame that something had extinguished or snuffed out.
Job is saying that graves are ready for him to mean that he will die soon. This is a mild way of referring to death.
17:2: Job is using the word If to introduce a question that anticipates a negative answer.
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is using one part of himself, his eye, to mean all of him in the act of seeing.
The implication is that Job’s friends have only been provoking him, not comforting him, because otherwise he would be able to recognize their comfort.
17:3: Job is speaking as if God would literally set down, that is, surrender to a court, something of value in order to guarantee Job’s appearance in court and good conduct. Job is similarly speaking as if God would literally be surety for him, that is, personally guarantee his appearance and conduct. Job speaks this way even though he says at the same time that God himself would be trying his case (that is the meaning of with you).
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is speaking of one person striking his hand against a second person’s hand as a symbolic action in order to show that he was committing himself to serve as a guarantor for that second person.
17:4: Job is speaking as if God had literally hidden the hearts of his friends in a place where their hearts would not come in contact with understanding. Within the context of this image, Job is using the heart to represent the mind.
Job is speaking as if God would literally exalt his friends or lift them up to a height. He means that God would honor them.

Job means implicitly that since God has kept his friends from understanding that he is innocent, God will not exalt or honor his friends by giving a guilty verdict against him, thereby vindicating what the friends have been saying. That would be allowing error to triumph.
17:5: לְחֵלֶק יַגִּיד רֵעִים וְעֵינֵי בָנָיו תִּכְלֶנָה
Job is using one thing that God does to maintain justice, punish those who commit perjury for a bribe, to represent all that God does to maintain justice.
Job is speaking of how the eyes of people who are dying fail (no longer see) in order to describe those people dying. This is a poetic way of speaking about death.
17:6: Job is using the word saying to mean that the peoples are citing him by name as an outstanding example of someone who seemed to be prospering because he was righteous but who came to ruin because he was actually wicked.
People were spitting in Job’s face as a symbolic action to show their contempt for him as a wicked person, which he appeared to them to be.
17:7: Job is using the term eye by association to mean sight.
The point of this comparison is that just as a shadow is insubstantial, so Job’s members, that is, the parts of his body, have become very thin.
17:9: Job is speaking of how God wants a person to live, or of the future that God has planned for a person, as if that were a way or path that God wants the person to walk along. When Job says that the righteous will hold his way, he means that that person will continue to walk along that path.
Job is speaking as if people who are innocent of wrongdoing have hands that are literally clean.
When Job says that innocent people will add strength, he means by this expression that they will continually grow stronger.
17:10: This phrase may be expressing a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word return tells in what way Job wants his friends to come.
17:11: Job is using the term days to refer to a specific time, his lifetime.
Job is speaking of his heart as if it were a living thing that could have desires.
17:12: Job is speaking about troubled times in life as if they were literally night and happy, prosperous times in life as if they were literally day.
Here the word face represents the presence of something, by association with the way that people can see the face of a person who is present.

Job may be using a proverb, a short, popular saying about something that is generally true in life, to summarize what his friends have been telling him. Or his friends may have been quoting this proverb themselves in their advice to Job.
17:13: Job is using the single activity of preparing a bed on which to sleep to mean all that is involved in making a place one’s home.
Job is using the term darkness to mean the realm of the dead, Sheol, by association with the way that it is dark there.
17:14: If Job said this, he would be saying that the pit was his home, by association with the way that a person lives in the home of his father.
If Job did speak this way to the pit, that is, to the realm of the dead, he would be speaking to something that he knew could not hear and understand him in order to make an emphatic statement.

If Job said this to a worm, such as would be found in a grave, he would be saying that the grave was going to be his home, by association with the way that a person shares a home with his mother and sister.
If Job did speak this way to a worm, he would be speaking to something that he knew could not hear and understand him in order to make an emphatic statement.

A worm is a small, legless creature that burrows through the ground, passing the soil through its digestive system in order to extract the nutrients that the soil contains. Worms also pass whatever else they find underground through their digestive systems, including dead bodies.
17:15: וְאַיֵּה אֵפוֹ תִקְוָתִי וְתִקְוָתִי מִי יְשׁוּרֶנָּה
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
17:16: בַּדֵּי שְׁאֹל תֵּרַדְנָה אִם־יַחַד עַל־עָפָר נָחַת
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is using the term bars to mean “gates,” by association with the way that bars keep a gate locked.
Job means implicitly that if his hope went down to the bars or gates of Sheol, it would be admitted there.
When Job speaks of having rest in the dust, he means having died. This is a poetic way of referring to death.
Job is speaking of his hope as if it were a living thing that could have rest.
18:2: Bildad is using the question form for emphasis.
Bildad is using the term words to mean what Job has been saying by using words. Bildad is answering Job by using the same language that Job used in 16:3.
18:3: Bildad is using the question form for emphasis.
Bildad is using this comparison to say that just as beasts have no understanding, so Job regards his friends as having no understanding.
Bildad is using the term eyes by association to mean sight. Sight, in turn, represents attention, perspective, and judgment.
18:4: Bildad is continuing to answer Job in his own words. In 16:9, Job spoke as if God were literally a wild animal that had torn him in his anger. Bildad is saying that it is actually Job who is tearing himself apart in his own anger.
Bildad is using the question form for emphasis.

Bildad is continuing to answer Job in his own words. In 14:18–19, Job said to God, “you destroy the hope of man,” and he compared that to the way “a rock moves from its place.” This could be a reference to an earthquake or a landslide. Bildad is implying that Job is being overly grandiose by comparing his individual situation with great natural events.
18:5: אוֹר רְשָׁעִים יִדְעָךְ וְלֹא־יִגַּהּ שְׁבִיב אִשּׁוֹ
Bildad is speaking of the happiness and prosperity of a wicked person as if those things were literally a light or flame.
18:6: אוֹר חָשַׁךְ בְּאָהֳלוֹ וְנֵרוֹ עָלָיו יִדְעָךְ

Bildad is continuing to speak of the happiness and prosperity of a wicked person as if those things were literally a light or lamp. He is also continuing to answer Job in his own words. In 17:12, Job said that his friends were telling him that light must be near because it was presently so dark in his life. Bildad is saying here in response that wicked people may be in the light, but soon it will become dark for them.
18:7: Bildad is using one sign of weakness, a shortening stride, to indicate weakness in general.
Bildad is speaking of a plan that a wicked person might make as if it were a living thing that could cast him down, that is, throw him or make him fall onto the ground.
18:8: Bildad is speaking as if a wicked person would literally be caught in a net or pitfall. He means that such a person will experience troubles that will keep him from fulfilling his plans.

Bildad is speaking of the feet of a wicked person as if they were a living thing that could cast him into a net. The implication seems to be that if the feet of the wicked person, rather than his eyes and his mind, are determining where he is going, he will walk into dangers unawares.

A pitfall is a type of trap for animals. To make it, people dig a pit in the ground and cover it with netting. They then put plant materials all over the netting to make it appear that the ground above the pit is just ordinary ground.
18:9: יֹאחֵז בְּעָקֵב פָּח יַחֲזֵק עָלָיו צַמִּים
Bildad is continuing to speak of a wicked person as if he would literally be caught in a snare or trap.

A snare was a device that people in this culture used to catch birds. It consisted of a loose loop of cord. A hunter would put seeds or other bait inside the loop. When a bird came inside the loop to eat the bait, the hunter would pull on the cord and catch the bird by its feet. A snare might also have a mechanism that a bird would trigger automatically by stepping inside the loop. Bildad is speaking as if this would happen to a wicked person, so that he would be caught by the heel.

By trap, Bildad means some other device for catching birds or animals. Interpreters are unsure exactly what this device is. The word Bildad uses suggests the idea of braiding, and so this could be a net of some kind.
18:10: טָמוּן בָּאָרֶץ חַבְלוֹ וּמַלְכֻּדְתּוֹ עֲלֵי נָתִיב
Bildad is continuing to speak of a wicked person as if he would literally be caught by a rope or trap.

By rope, Bildad means some further device for catching birds or animals. He seems to mean some larger device for catching animals that would work the same way as a “snare” that catches birds. A hunter might hide a loop of rope in the ground and pull on the rope to catch an animal once it stepped inside the loop.
It is unclear whether Bildad is talking about a specific type of trap here. He may be using a general term for any device that would catch a bird or animal.
18:11: Bildad is speaking of these Terrors as if they were a living thing that could chase a wicked person the way a dog or wolf would, nipping at his feet to disable him so that he could not run away to safety.
18:12: Bildad is speaking of the strength of a wicked person as if it were a living thing that could become hungry. He means that a wicked person’s strength becomes weakened as if by hunger.
Bildad is speaking as if disaster were literally at the side of a wicked person. He means that it will strike him as soon as there is opportunity.
18:13: The expression the firstborn of death means the strongest kind of death or a terrible kind of death.
18:14: If terror is indeed the agent that Bildad says pulls the wicked person from his tent, then Bildad is speaking of terror as if it were a living thing that could do this. He actually means that the disasters that cause a wicked person to feel terror also deprive him of safety and security.

If the pronoun one does refer to terror, then Bildad is speaking of terror as if it were a living thing, a soldier, who could march a captured enemy to his king as a prisoner. Once again Bildad would be using terror to mean the disasters that cause a wicked person to feel terror.
Like the expression “the firstborn of death” in the previous verse, the expression the king of terrors here is a superlative. It means the worst terror there is, specifically, death.
18:15: Bildad means implicitly that the tent will no longer belong to the wicked person, probably because he will be dead (a prisoner of the “king of terrors,” death, as the previous verse describes).
18:16: מִתַּחַת שָׁרָשָׁיו יִבָשׁוּ וּמִמַּעַל יִמַּל קְצִירוֹ
Bildad is speaking as if the wicked person were literally a tree that dies from lack of moisture.
18:17: Bildad is using the term earth by association to mean the people who live on the earth.
Here, name represents a person’s fame and reputation.
Bildad is speaking as if the surface of the land or ground were literally its face.
18:18: Bildad is using the term light to represent life and the term darkness to represent death.
18:20: עַל־יוֹמוֹ נָשַׁמּוּ אַחֲרֹנִים וְקַדְמֹנִים אָחֲזוּ שָׂעַר

Bildad is using two groups of people to mean all people. This could mean: (1) people who live after God punishes the wicked person and people who were alive beforehand and recognized that God would punish the wicked person; (2) people who live to the west of the wicked person and people who live to the east of the wicked person.
Bildad is using the term day to mean what happens to the wicked person at a particular time, the time when God punishes him.
Bildad is speaking as if horror were literally an object that people could seize.
18:21: אַךְ־אֵלֶּה מִשְׁכְּנוֹת עַוָּל וְזֶה מְקוֹם לֹא־יָדַע־אֵל
Bildad is speaking as if all the misfortunes he has described were literally the dwellings of wicked people, the place where they live.
19:2: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is using one part of himself, his soul, to mean all of him.
Job is speaking as if his friends could literally crush him with their words.
Job is using the term words to mean what his friends have been saying by using words.
19:3: The expression ten times means “many times,” not literally ten times, no more and no less.
The phrases you are not ashamed and you mistreat me together convey a single idea.
19:4: Interpreters are not certain what Job means by this statement. He could mean: (1) that any sin he might have committed would be his own private concern.
19:6: Job is speaking as if a net that God had set as a trap had literally closed around him. Job is answering Bildad in his own words, but Job is making the net a symbol of the unjust punishment of the innocent rather than of the just punishment of the wicked.
19:7: The expression Violence! refers generally to mistreatment, including but not limited to actual violence.
19:8: Job is speaking of his life as if it were a way or path that he was walking along, and he is speaking as if God had built a wall to block that path so that he could not continue on it.

In a parallel image, Job is speaking of his activities as if they were paths on which he was walking, and he is speaking as if God had made it so dark on those paths that he could not walk on them because he could not see where he was going.
19:9: Job is speaking as if the glory or honor that he formerly had were literally an article of clothing that God had stripped from him.
Job is speaking as if he had formerly been wearing an actual crown, a symbol of ruling authority, and that God had removed that crown from his head.

Job is using this expression to describe his lifetime. He means the period extending from his earliest days of life to the present.
27:7: In this culture, people would make clear that they did not want something to happen to them by saying they wanted it to happen to their enemies. That showed that it was the opposite of what they wanted for themselves.
Job is speaking as if this person were literally rising up, that is, standing up from a seating or lying position, in order to attack him.
27:8: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
27:9: הַצַעֲקָתוֹ יִשְׁמַע ׀ אֵל כִּי־תָבוֹא עָלָיו צָרָה
Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is using the term hear in a specific sense to mean “answer.”
Job is speaking of trouble as if it were a living thing that could come upon a wicked person (for example, as an animal might pounce on its prey).
27:10: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
27:11: Here, hand represents the activity of a person by association with the way that people use their hands to do things.

Job is not using this expression to suggest that there are certain things with the Almighty, that is, objects that are in his presence. Rather, the expression refers to the things that pertain to the Almighty, meaning his characteristic ways of doing things. In this context, the expression refers to the way that the Almighty actually treats the wicked.
27:12: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
For emphasis, Job is using a construction in which a subject and its verb come from the same root.
27:13: Job is speaking as if the punishment that God assigns to a wicked man were literally a portion or share of goods that God allotted to that person.
Job is speaking as if the punishment that the Almighty assigns to oppressors were literally a heritage or inheritance that he leaves to them.
27:14: Job is using the term sword by association to mean death, since in this culture people killed others with swords.
Job is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general.
27:15: The term death could mean: (1) death literally; (2) a plague, in which case Job would be using a general term for death to mean one specific cause of death. There is a similar use in Jeremiah 15:2. In that case Job could also be speaking as if the plague itself had buried this survivor, meaning that it had caused his death.
This could mean: (1) the wicked person’s last surviving descendant; (2) not a specific survivor but his surviving descendants in general.
In this culture, a man might marry more than one woman, so by widows, Job means implicitly that this “wicked man” had more than one wife.
27:16: יִצְבֹּר כֶּעָפָר כָּסֶף וְכַחֹמֶר יָכִין מַלְבּוּשׁ
The point of this comparison is that just as dust is abundant and clay mounds contain great quantities of clay, so a wicked person might acquire silver in abundance and clothing in great quantities.
Job is using one valuable commodity, silver, to represent wealth in general.
27:18: בָּנָה כָעָשׁ בֵּיתוֹ וּכְסֻכָּה עָשָׂה נֹצֵר

The point of these comparisons is that the house of a moth, that is, its cocoon, is very fragile, as is a hut that a guard would build in a field out of branches to watch over crops during harvest time.
בָּנָה כָעָשׁ בֵּיתוֹ וּכְסֻכָּה עָשָׂה נֹצֵר
While the actual house of a wicked person might become abandoned and collapse from neglect, Job could be using the term house to represent the life of that person.

A moth is a flying insect that is typically active at night. It begins life as a wingless larva. The larva eventually spins a silk cocoon around itself, and inside that cocoon, it changes into a flying moth.
27:19: Job is speaking of going to sleep and waking up by association with things that people do when they go to sleep (lie down in bed) and wake up (open their eyes).

Job is making an overstatement to emphasize how quickly a wicked person loses his wealth. He is speaking as if that person would go to sleep rich and wake up with nothing, that is, as if he would lose all of his riches in a single night.
This expression means that the wicked person no longer has any possessions.
27:20: Job is speaking as if a storm would literally carry a wicked person away. He means that that person perishes as quickly and unexpectedly as he would if a storm carried him away.
27:21: Job is continuing to speak as if a wind would literally pick up a wicked person and carry him away.
Job lived in a place where there was desert to the east, so he is referring implicitly to a strong, hot wind coming from the desert.
27:22: Job is speaking of this wind as if it were a living thing that could hurl itself upon a wicked person and not pity him, that is, not show him any mercy.
27:23: In this culture, people would clap their hands together as a symbolic action to express negative emotions such as grief, indignation, or derision. In this context, Job is speaking as if the wind were expressing derision at the wicked person.
In this culture, people would make a hissing sound in order to express derision. Job is speaking as if the wind were also expressing derision at the wicked person by making such a sound.

This could mean: (1) that the wind Job is describing hisses at the wicked person from within the home that it has forced him to abandon. (Job says of the wind in verse 21, “it blasts him from his place.”); (2) that the wind hisses at the wicked person now that he is out of his place.
28:2: Job is using one part of the ground, the dust on its surface, to mean the ground itself. Iron is actually taken from deep in the ground.
Job is speaking of the ore from which copper is smelted as stone, since that ore is a type of stone.
The term “smelt” means to break ore into pieces and to use great heat to melt it so that a metal such as copper will separate from it.
28:3: Job means implicitly that the person he is describing either brings lights underground, where there is otherwise darkness, or opens a mineshaft that lets light in.
Job says every here as a generalization for emphasis.
The terms gloom and deep darkness mean similar things. Job is using the two terms together for emphasis.
Job is using the phrase gloom and deep darkness by association to mean deep underground, where it is very dark.
28:4: Job is speaking of a foot as if it were a living thing that could be unaware of something. (That is what the term forgotten indicates here.) This could be describing: (1) the location of the mines. Job would be saying that they are in remote places where people do not go. In that case the word foot would represent people traveling; (2) the way that people walk on the ground above mines without realizing that miners are at work deep below them.
Job means implicitly that these miners dangle and swing from ropes in order to get down into the mines. He is emphasizing the risks that people will take in order to find precious metals.
28:5: Job is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general.
Job is speaking as if miners literally overturned the earth, that is, put on top what had been on the bottom. He is speaking generally of how miners reshape the terrain in which they work.

Job assumes that his friends will understand that he is using the term fire to refer to an ancient mining practice. Miners would build fires against the walls of mines to heat the rock. They would then splash water against the heated rock to cause it to crack. This allowed them to extract ore more readily.
28:6: A sapphire is a rare and valuable blue gemstone.
28:7: Job is referring implicitly to the path that miners take into the depths of the earth in search of gemstones and precious metals.
Job is using one part of a falcon, its eye, to mean all of it in the act of seeing.
A falcon is a bird that eats animals and other birds.
28:8: The expression son of describes a person or animal that possesses a certain quality. The word pride indicates that the animals Job is describing are confident in their strength and fierceness and are not afraid of other animals.
28:9: The expression “stretch out one’s hand against” means to attack something. Job is saying that miners will attack, that is, break up even the hardest kinds of rock in search of valuable materials.
Job is speaking of the ground below mountains as if it were the roots of those mountains.
Job is speaking as if miners literally turn entire mountains upside down. He may be using the term mountains to represent great quantities of material.
28:10: Job is using one part of a miner, his eye, to mean all of him in the act of seeing.
Job says every here as a generalization for emphasis.
28:11: מִבְּכִי נְהָרוֹת חִבֵּשׁ וְתַעֲלֻמָהּ יֹצִא אוֹר

Job is speaking as if a miner literally binds streams of water to keep them from flowing. He means that miners temporarily dam up streams or divert their flow to expose the materials that their waters usually hide.
Job is using the term light by association to describe something that is in view, since people need light in order to see things.
28:12: וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם בִּינָה
Job is speaking as if wisdom, which he also calls understanding, could literally be found in a place.
וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם בִּינָה
Job is not using the question form simply for emphasis. He wants his listeners to consider these questions in light of what he has just said.
וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם בִּינָה
Job is drawing an implicit comparison between the difficulty of finding gemstones and precious metals and the even greater difficulty of finding wisdom and understanding.
וְהַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא וְאֵי זֶה מְקוֹם בִּינָה
These two phrases mean similar things. Job is using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.
28:13: The word translated disposition could mean implicitly: (1) where God has put wisdom; (2) the value of wisdom.
28:14: תְּהוֹם אָמַר לֹא בִי־הִיא וְיָם אָמַר אֵין עִמָּדִי
Job is speaking of the deep (that is, the depths of the ocean) and of the sea (probably meaning its broad expanse) as if they were living things that could speak.
תְּהוֹם אָמַר לֹא בִי־הִיא וְיָם אָמַר אֵין עִמָּדִי
These two phrases mean similar things. Job is using repetition to emphasize the idea that the phrases express.
28:16: An onyx is a valuable gemstone that comes in many colors but is best known in its black color.
28:17: The term crystal could be describing: (1) a beautiful natural form that a clear or colored mineral might take, allowing light to shine through it.
28:18: Coral is a beautiful, hard substance that grows on ocean reefs.
The word jasper describes a precious stone, often reddish-brown, that often has streaks and markings of other colors.
The word rubies describes brilliant gemstones that are often deep red.
28:19: The word topaz describes a valuable gemstone that is often blue or yellow.
The word Cush is the name of a place. It is the ancient name for the upper Nile region.
28:21: Job is using one part of a living thing, its eyes, to mean all of it in the act of seeing.
28:22: אֲבַדּוֹן וָמָוֶת אָמְרוּ בְּאָזְנֵינוּ שָׁמַעְנוּ שִׁמְעָהּ
Job is speaking as if Abaddon and death were living things that could speak.
אֲבַדּוֹן וָמָוֶת אָמְרוּ בְּאָזְנֵינוּ שָׁמַעְנוּ שִׁמְעָהּ

The terms Abaddon and death mean similar things. As a note to 26:6 explains, Abaddon is another name for Sheol, the abode of the dead. In this context, the term death likely refers by association to the abode of the dead. Job is using the two terms together for emphasis.
28:23: אֱלֹהִים הֵבִין דַּרְכָּהּ וְהוּא יָדַע אֶת־מְקוֹמָהּ
Job is continuing to speak as if wisdom could literally be found in a place and that there was a way to get there.
28:24: הוּא לִקְצוֹת־הָאָרֶץ יַבִּיט תַּחַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמַיִם יִרְאֶה
Job is using the two main components of creation, earth and the heavens, to mean the entire creation.
28:25: Job is referring implicitly to the rain waters that clouds contain.
Job is speaking as if God literally used a measure in order to put the right amount of rain waters in the clouds.
28:26: Job is using the expression the flash of the thunders by association to mean the bolts of lightning that accompany thunder.
28:28: The Lord is speaking as if people should physically turn away from evil. He means that if people want to have understanding, they should not live in an evil way but instead live in a good way.
29:2: Job is using the terms months and days to refer to a specific time.
29:3: בְּהִלּוֹ נֵרוֹ עֲלֵי רֹאשִׁי לְאוֹרוֹ אֵלֶךְ חֹשֶׁךְ
Job is speaking as if God literally shone a lamp above and around him so that he could see where to walk even in the darkness.

Job is using one part of himself, his head, to mean all of him when speaking as if God shone a lamp above and around him. He is probably speaking of himself in terms of his head because that would have been the part of him closest to the lamp.
29:4: Job is using the term days to refer to a specific time.
Job is speaking as if God’s friendship were literally an object that had rested upon his tent.
As the next two verses indicate, Job is referring to his family by association with the tent in which they lived and to his possessions by association with the same tent, in which he kept them.
29:6: בִּרְחֹץ הֲלִיכַי בְּחֵמָה וְצוּר יָצוּק עִמָּדִי פַּלְגֵי־שָׁמֶן

Job is speaking as if his herds used to produce so much milk that there was butter everywhere he went, so that when he walked anywhere, it was as if his feet were literally being bathed in butter. He is also speaking as if his olive trees used to produce so many olives that it was as if there were literally streams of oil coming to him out of the rocks.
29:7: Taking a seat in the public square by the city gate was a symbolic action by which Job showed that he was a recognized community leader, a member of the council that settled legal matters for the city residents.
29:8: This expression does not mean that these young men looked for hiding places where no one would find them. It means that they moved back from the place where the leaders sat, blending into the crowd. The idea is that before Job came, they thought they might have something to contribute to the deliberations after their elders had spoken, as Elihu does in this book starting in chapter 32. But once Job arrived, they knew that his wise counsel would settle matters and they would have no need or opportunity to contribute.
Rising and standing when Job arrived was a symbolic action that showed respect for his wisdom and place in the community.
The terms rose and stood mean similar things. Job is using the two terms together for emphasis.
29:9: Job is using the term words to mean what these princes had been saying by using words before he arrived.

Covering the mouth with the hand prevents a person from speaking. While the princes could simply have stopped talking without doing that, they did it as a symbolic action to show respect for Job, indicating that there was nothing they could say that would be more valuable than what he would say.
29:10: Job is speaking as if the tongue of each noble literally stuck to his palate, that is, to the roof of his mouth. He means that they did not say anything, as no one could say anything if his tongue truly had become stuck in this way.
29:11: Job is using one part of each of these community members, his ear, to mean all of him in the act of hearing.
Job means implicitly that the people blessed him for giving such wise, godly counsel.
Job is using the term eye by association to mean sight. Sight, in turn, represents attention, perspective, and judgment.
29:13: Job is speaking of the blessing that he received from someone who was perishing as if it were a living thing that could come upon him.
Job is using one part of a widow, her heart, to mean all of her in the act of feeling joy. Here the heart represents the feelings.
29:14: Job is speaking as if he literally clothed himself with righteousness during the time that he is describing. In this context, the image of clothing represents the character of a person.
In this comparison, clothing once again represents the character of a person.
29:15: עֵינַיִם הָיִיתִי לַעִוֵּר וְרַגְלַיִם לַפִּסֵּחַ אָנִי
Job is speaking as if he had literally been eyes and feet that other people needed.
29:16: Job is speaking as if he had literally been a father to needy people. He means that he fulfilled the role of a father by being a protector and advocate.

Job is referring implicitly to a case whose details he did not know before someone brought it to the city gate for adjudication. Job did not know these details because he was not personally acquainted with the person bringing the case. So he was not motivated by friendship or family loyalty, but simply by the interests of justice.
29:17: וָאֲשַׁבְּרָה מְתַלְּעוֹת עַוָּל וּמִשִּׁנָּיו אַשְׁלִיךְ טָרֶף

Job is speaking as if an unrighteous person had been a wild animal that was holding a vulnerable person like captured prey in its teeth and as if he had broken the jaws of this animal so that they could no longer hold the vulnerable person, who would drop out to safety.
29:18: Job is speaking of his home as if it were literally a nest such as a bird would live in.
The point of this comparison is that just as sand consists of a very large number of grains, so Job expected to live for a very large number of days.
29:19: שָׁרְשִׁי פָתוּחַ אֱלֵי־מָיִם וְטַל יָלִין בִּקְצִירִי
Job spoke of himself in those days as if he were literally a tree that was healthy and flourishing because it was getting all the moisture that it required.
Job was speaking as if the dew had been a traveler that had found lodging for the night on a branch of the tree that he was using to represent himself.
29:20: Job means implicitly that the glory or honor that he enjoys is always fresh because people keep honoring him in new ways.

Job is speaking as if he had a bow, a weapon that he used with arrows, and that it grew freshly in his hand the way that a branch sprouts from a tree trunk. (Job uses the same verb for “sprout” in 14:7–9 to describe a tree reviving and sending out shoots when moisture returns to the ground.) He means that the bow, which represents his strength, is lively and vigorous.
29:22: Job is using the term word to mean what he said by using words.

Job is speaking as if his speech literally dripped, that is, fell in drops, on his listeners. He means that it was refreshing and invigorating to them, like gentle rain. This enabled them to recognize that he was giving sound advice.
29:23: The point of this comparison is that just as people are eager for rain to fall and water their crops, so Job’s listeners were eager to hear him speak.

Job is using a complex image here. First, he is speaking as if the people listening to him were literally the ground. Second, he is speaking of the ground soaking up rainfall as if it were opening its mouth to drink water. Job does not mean that the people opened their mouths to speak; he is actually describing them listening.

In the region where the book of Job was composed, people would plant crops in the fall. Rain at that time would help the crops start growing. But farmers depended on later rains, which would fall in the spring after an interval during which little rain fell, to enable the crops grow to maturity.
29:24: Job is describing one thing he did to encourage despondent people, he smiled on them, to mean all that he did to encourage them.

Job is speaking as if there had been light shining from his face. He is describing a cheerful facial expression that indicated hope and a favorable disposition. Job is also using a further characteristic image for facial expressions. In this culture, people would say that someone “lifted up” his face if he made a cheerful expression but that his face “fell” if he made a gloomy expression. Job means that he did not let the situations of the people he wanted to help discourage him. Job is combining the two images and saying that they did not cause the light of his face to fall.
29:25: Job is speaking of what he determined his community should do as if that were a way or path for the people to walk along.
Job is describing how he held the position of a chief by association with the way he sat in a place reserved for such a leader.

In this culture, kings would accompany their armies into the field as their commanders. The point of this comparison is probably that just as the authority of a king would be unquestioned within his army, so people did not question Job’s directions as their leader.
Job makes this further comparison to specify that he led the community gently and in its own best interests. He did not exercise his authority in an arbitrary, despotic way.
30:1: The implications of this statement is that the fathers of the young men who now laugh at Job were shiftless and incompetent. This could mean: (1) that Job would not employ these men to do even such menial tasks as shepherd dogs do; (2) that Job would not specifically employ these men as shepherds for his flocks, working with his sheepdogs.
30:2: Job is using the question form for emphasis.
Job is using one part of these young men, their hands, to mean all of them in the act of using strength to work. As the rest of the verse indicates, these young men have only feeble strength.

Job is speaking of old age as if it were a living thing that has perished in these young men. Eliphaz uses the same term for “old age” in 5:26. There it means the maturity and accomplishment that come from a long life well lived. Here the term seems to indicate the vigor that someone would have in his youth that would enable him to live such a long life.
30:3: Job is speaking of the dry land by association to mean the roots that grow in the land, as the next verse makes clear. It may also be helpful to begin a new sentence here.
The term yesterday could mean: (1) time gone by; (2) the darkness of the night that precedes day.
This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word desolation tells what kind of waste this is.
30:4: The word mallow describes a kind of flowering plant whose leaves are edible.
A broom tree is a kind of shrub that grows in desert areas.

Job is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general. While the roots of the broom tree are edible, they have a bitter taste, and only a desperate person would eat them. So there is a sense here that the people whom Job is describing eat these roots out of desperation.
30:5: Job means implicitly that these young men are driven out from the midst of human community.

Job is speaking of people chasing others away, so this seems to be a reference to people shouting at a would-be thief in order to call attention to him and get him to flee before he steals something. Job is probably not referring to people shouting to get others to pursue and apprehend a thief who has already stolen something.
30:6: Job is using one part of the ground, the dust on its surface, to mean the ground itself. Iron is actually taken from deep in the ground.
30:7: Job is speaking as if these young men literally bray as if they were donkeys. He likely means that they moan with hunger, as wild animals cry out when they need food.
30:8: In this context, the expression sons of describes people who share the qualities of something. Job is using this expression to describe the behavior and character of these young men. The word fool here does not indicate someone who lacks intelligence or education; it means someone who chooses to disobey God, thinking there will be no consequences. The word name here means a good reputation.
Job is using one means by which authorities might drive such young men out of the community, by scourging (whipping) them, to mean all of the ways in which they would drive them out.
30:9: Job means implicitly that these young men are singing about him disrespectfully.

The meaning of the term word here is the same as the meaning of the term “saying” in 17:6. Job means that these young men are citing him by name as an outstanding example of someone who seemed to be prospering because he was righteous but who came to ruin because he was actually wicked.
30:10: Staying away from Job, that is, not approaching him or speaking with him, was a symbolic action that conveyed disrespect and disapproval. Even though physically it was the same thing that young men formerly did to show respect for Job, discreetly withdrawing from his presence, now it had the opposite meaning.
Spitting in Job’s face was a symbolic action that showed contempt for him as someone who was presumably a sinner.

Job does not mean that these young men spit at him from a distance, even though he says that they stay away from him. He means that when they must unavoidably pass near him, they use the occasion to spit in his face.
30:11: Job is speaking as if God has in some way literally loosed a cord that belongs to him or pertains to him. This could mean: (1) that God has loosened the bowstring on a bow that belongs to Job, so that the bow is no longer useful. The bow would represent Job’s strength; (2) that God has released a cord that was holding up the tent in which Job lived, so that the tent has collapsed. The tent would represent Job’s life.
Job is speaking as if restraint were literally an object that people could cast away.
Here the word face represents the presence of a person by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.
30:12: The right side was usually the most dangerous side on which to approach an enemy soldier, since a majority of soldiers were right-handed and would use their right hands and arms to wield their swords. The implication is that these young men have no fear of what Job might do to them.
Job is speaking of these young men as if they were the brood of a bird or animal. The image is of a cluster of immature offspring moving agitatedly about.

Job is using one part of himself, his foot, to mean all of him in the act of walking. He probably means that as he is walking on the road, when these young men are approaching from the opposite direction, they do not stand respectfully aside so that he can pass. Instead, they shove him out of the way so that they can pass. When young men traveling in the same direction overtake him, they similarly push him aside so that they can go by.
Job is speaking of siege mounds by association with the way that they provide roads or ways for attacking armies to get into cities and cause their destruction.
Job is speaking as if he were a city and these young men were literally building siege mounds in order to conquer that city.
30:13: Job is speaking as if there were literally a path that he could take to escape from the attacks of these young men and that they are destroying it so that Job cannot use it.

Job is speaking as if calamity were literally an object that these young men could move forward, farther along its route to a destination. He means that in addition to all the bad things that have happened to him, they do further bad things to him.
This could mean: (1) that they do despicable things to Job that no decent person would join them in doing; (2) that they are contemptible people. This may be a popular expression indicating that.
30:14: כְּפֶרֶץ רָחָב יֶאֱתָיוּ תַּחַת שֹׁאָה הִתְגַּלְגָּלוּ

Job is continuing the image of himself as a city and these young men as a besieging army. He is describing an attack in full force: The army has made a wide breach in the city wall and the soldiers are pouring through it. Job says within this image that they roll on, perhaps like waves of the sea, one wave after another.
30:15: Job is speaking of these Terrors as if they were living things that could pursue him.
The point of this comparison is that just as a strong wind relentlessly drives away light objects, so the Terrors that Job is experiencing are relentlessly depriving him of dignity.
The point of this comparison is that just as a cloud fades from the sky, so all hope of deliverance has faded for Job.
30:16: Job is speaking as if his life were a liquid that was being poured out of a container so that soon none of it would be left in the container.
Job is speaking of these days as if they were living things that could seize him.
30:17: Job is speaking of Night as if it were a living thing that could pierce his bones. He is doing this to describe the pain that he feels more keenly at night.
Job is using one part of himself, his bones, to mean all of him in the act of feeling pain.
Job is speaking as if pain were literally piercing his body or putting holes in it. He means that he gets a stabbing sensation of pain as if he were actually being stabbed.

It is not entirely clear what Job means by this expression. He uses the same expression in 30:30 to describe how his skin, darkened by disease, is peeling off. So this could be a reference to the pain from his sores radiating deep into his body.
Job is speaking of the pains he is suffering as if they were living things that could be gnawing him and could rest (although they do not).
30:18: Job is referring implicitly to the great force of his skin disease, its power to do so much damage.

Job is using the term visited in a particular sense. 31:18: Job says from my youth and from the belly of my mother as overstatements for emphasis.

Job is using the term gate by association to mean the community court, which would hold its sessions in the public square near the city gate.
31:24: If Job had spoken to fine gold in this way, he would have been speaking to something that he knew could not hear him in order to show in a strong way how he felt about it.

Job is using one part of himself, his hand, to mean all of him in the act of acquiring wealth.
31:26: Job is using the term light by association to mean the sun.

31:27: Job is speaking as if his hand were a living thing that could have kissed his mouth. This expression refers to an opponent in a legal proceeding.

Job is using the question form for emphasis.

31:37: Job is speaking of his actions as if they were steps along a path that he had been walking along.

Job is speaking of the soil on his land and its furrows as if they were living things that could cry out for justice and weep because of oppression.

The Lord is using the question form for emphasis.

41:15: The Lord is speaking as if the scales of Leviathan were literally shields.

41:17: The Lord is speaking as if a scale were literally a man and the scale next to it were literally his brother.

41:20: The Lord is using the term blown by association to mean a fire that someone has blown or fanned to make it burn hot.

This phrase expresses a single idea by using two words connected with and. The word reed tells what kind of fuel the fire is burning that is heating the pot. People would make a fire out of dried reeds if they wanted it to burn hot quickly, although for a short time, such as to boil water.
41:22: The Lord is speaking as if strength were a living thing that could stay for the night in the neck of Leviathan.
The Lord is speaking of fear as if it were a living thing that could leap up in front of Leviathan.
Here the word face represents the presence of a person by association with the way people can see the face of someone who is present.

The Lord is referring to the underbelly of Leviathan as the folds of its flesh. In most animals, this area is soft and vulnerable, but in Leviathan it is tight and secure.

The point of this comparison is that just as straw is flimsy and rotten wood falls apart, so Leviathan considers iron to be flimsy and bronze to be a substance that would fall apart.

41:29: The Lord is speaking as if Leviathan could intelligently make judgments about the strength of weapons that people might use against it.

41:33: The Lord is using one part of the earth, the dust on its surface, to mean the earth itself.

In this context, the expression sons of describes something that shares the qualities of something else. The Lord is using this expression to describe the behavior and character of certain creatures. The Lord is speaking as if Leviathan were literally a king. He means that no other animal can challenge Leviathan.

42:6: By the word despise, Job does not mean that he hates something. He means that he thinks little of something. He could mean: (1) that he thinks little of himself, that is, he no longer believes that he can credibly declare whether God is treating anyone fairly or unfairly; (2) that he now thinks little of what he said in all of his speeches.

In this culture, people would sprinkle dust and ashes on themselves as a symbolic action to show that they were greatly distressed. This is what Job’s friends were doing in 2:12 when they threw dust into the air so that it would land on their heads. Job was doing something similar in 2:8 when he sat down in a pile of ashes. Job could be sprinkling dust and ashes from the pile on himself as he speaks these words, or he could be speaking as if he were doing that in order to describe how sincerely he is repenting.

The author is using one kind of food, bread, to mean food in general.

42:14: The expression called the name is the way people in this culture spoke of giving a child a name when the child was born.

It was not customary in this culture for fathers to give their daughters an inheritance. The author may mention this because it shows the special love and regard that Job had for his daughters.

This expression could mean: (1) that Job gave his daughters an inheritance just as he did for his sons; (2) that Job gave his daughters as an inheritance land that was located in the same area as land that he gave to his sons as their inheritance.

42:17: The author is speaking as if days were an object and as if Job were a container that was full of them.
The expressions old and full of days mean similar things. The author is using them together for emphasis.
